:::lede
This chapter collects three subjects that extend the algebra of the earlier chapters: the arithmetic of commutative rings, leading to unique factorization; Galois theory, which connects field extensions to group theory; and an introduction to Lie groups and Lie algebras, the continuous analogues of finite groups and their representations. These topics go beyond the course on which this book is based, and the chapter is a survey. Some of the deeper theorems are stated without proof, and we say so each time.
:::

In this section all rings are commutative with identity (Definition [4.1.1](/notes/math-55a/4-1-rings-and-fields#definition-4-1-1)).

## <span class="num">17.1.1</span> Ideals and Quotient Rings

Recall from Chapter 10 that an ***ideal*** of a ring $R$ is an additive subgroup $I \subseteq R$ such that $ra \in I$ for all $r \in R$ and $a \in I$. For $a \in R$, the ***principal ideal*** generated by $a$ is $(a) = aR = \{ra : r \in R\}$. More generally, for $a_1, \ldots, a_n \in R$, the set $$(a_1, \ldots, a_n) = \{r_1 a_1 + \cdots + r_n a_n : r_1, \ldots, r_n \in R\}$$ is the smallest ideal containing $a_1, \ldots, a_n$, the ideal ***generated*** by them. We say that $a$ ***divides*** $b$, written $a \mid b$, if $b = ac$ for some $c \in R$; equivalently, $(b) \subseteq (a)$.

:::definition{17.1.1} Quotient ring
Let $I$ be an ideal of $R$. The ***quotient ring*** $R/I$ is the quotient group of $(R, +)$ by $I$, whose elements are the cosets $a + I$, with the multiplication $(a + I)(b + I) = ab + I$.
:::

The multiplication is well defined: if $a' = a + x$ and $b' = b + y$ with $x, y \in I$, then $a'b' = ab + (ay + xb + xy) \in ab + I$. The ring axioms for $R/I$ follow from those for $R$, and the projection $R \to R/I$, $a \mapsto a + I$, is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel $I$.

:::proposition{17.1.2} Kernels and quotients
Let $\varphi : R \to S$ be a ring homomorphism. Then $\ker \varphi$ is an ideal of $R$, $\Img \varphi$ is a subring of $S$, and $a + \ker \varphi \mapsto \varphi(a)$ is an isomorphism of rings $R/\ker \varphi \to \Img \varphi$.
:::

:::proof
The kernel is an additive subgroup, and if $a \in \ker \varphi$ and $r \in R$, then $\varphi(ra) = \varphi(r) \cdot 0 = 0$. The image is closed under addition and multiplication and contains $\varphi(1) = 1$. By the First Isomorphism Theorem (Theorem [3.3.3](/notes/math-55a/3-3-the-isomorphism-theorems#theorem-3-3-3)) for the additive groups, the map $a + \ker \varphi \mapsto \varphi(a)$ is a well-defined isomorphism of additive groups onto $\Img \varphi$. It respects multiplication because $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$, and it sends $1 + \ker \varphi$ to $1$.
:::

:::definition{17.1.3} Integral domain
A ring $R$ with $1 \neq 0$ is an ***integral domain*** if it has no zero divisors: $ab = 0$ implies $a = 0$ or $b = 0$.
:::

In an integral domain we may cancel nonzero factors: if $ab = ac$ and $a \neq 0$, then $a(b - c) = 0$, so $b = c$.

:::definition{17.1.4} Prime and maximal ideals
Let $I \neq R$ be an ideal of $R$. Then $I$ is ***prime*** if $ab \in I$ implies $a \in I$ or $b \in I$, and ***maximal*** if the only ideals $J$ with $I \subseteq J \subseteq R$ are $I$ and $R$.
:::

:::proposition{17.1.5} Quotients by prime and maximal ideals
Let $I \neq R$ be an ideal of $R$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $R/I$ is an integral domain if and only if $I$ is prime.
2. $R/I$ is a field if and only if $I$ is maximal.

In particular, every maximal ideal is prime.
:::

:::proof
Note that $1 + I \neq 0 + I$, since $1 \notin I$.

(i) In $R/I$, we have $(a + I)(b + I) = 0$ if and only if $ab \in I$, and $a + I = 0$ if and only if $a \in I$.

(ii) Suppose $R/I$ is a field, and let $J \supsetneq I$ be an ideal. Choose $a \in J \setminus I$. Then $a + I$ has an inverse $b + I$, so $ab - 1 \in I \subseteq J$, and $1 = ab - (ab - 1) \in J$; hence $J = R$. Conversely, suppose $I$ is maximal and $a \notin I$. The ideal $I + (a) = \{x + ra : x \in I, r \in R\}$ strictly contains $I$, so it is $R$, and $1 = x + ab$ for some $x \in I$ and $b \in R$. Then $(a + I)(b + I) = 1 + I$.

The last statement holds because a field has no zero divisors.
:::

## <span class="num">17.1.2</span> Divisibility in Integral Domains

:::example{17.1.6} Integral domains
Every field is an integral domain, and so is every subring of a field. For instance $\ZZ$, the Gaussian integers ${\ZZ}[i] = \{a + bi : a, b \in \ZZ\}$, and ${\ZZ}[\sqrt{-5}] = \{a + b\sqrt{-5} : a, b \in \ZZ\}$ are subrings of $\CC$, hence integral domains. If $k$ is a field, then $k[x]$ is an integral domain, since $\deg(fg) = \deg f + \deg g$ for nonzero $f, g$. The ring $\ZZ/6$ is not an integral domain, since $2 \cdot 3 = 0$.
:::

:::definition{17.1.7} Units, associates, irreducible and prime elements
Let $R$ be an integral domain.

- A ***unit*** is an element $u \in R$ with a multiplicative inverse: $uv = 1$ for some $v \in R$. The units form a group $R^\times$ under multiplication.
- Two elements $a, b$ are ***associates*** if $a = ub$ for some unit $u$.
- A nonzero non-unit $p \in R$ is ***irreducible*** if $p = ab$ implies that $a$ or $b$ is a unit.
- A nonzero non-unit $p \in R$ is ***prime*** if $p \mid ab$ implies $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$.
:::

In an integral domain, $a$ and $b$ are associates if and only if $(a) = (b)$: if $a = bc$ and $b = ad$, then $a = acd$, so either $a = b = 0$ or $cd = 1$. A nonzero element $p$ is prime if and only if $(p)$ is a prime ideal.

:::proposition{17.1.8} Prime implies irreducible
In an integral domain, every prime element is irreducible.
:::

:::proof
Suppose $p$ is prime and $p = ab$. Then $p \mid ab$, so $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$; say $a = pc$. Then $p = pcb$, and canceling $p \neq 0$ gives $1 = cb$, so $b$ is a unit.
:::

:::note
The converse fails in general: in ${\ZZ}[\sqrt{-5}]$ the element $2$ is irreducible but not prime (Example [17.1](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings)). It holds in principal ideal domains (Theorem [17.1](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings)).
:::

## <span class="num">17.1.3</span> Euclidean Domains

:::definition{17.1.9} Euclidean domain
An integral domain $R$ is a ***Euclidean domain*** if there is a function $N : R \setminus \{0\} \to \ZZ_{\geq 0}$, a ***Euclidean function***, such that for all $a, b \in R$ with $b \neq 0$ there exist $q, r \in R$ with $$a = bq + r, \qquad \text{where } r = 0 \text{ or } N(r) < N(b).$$
:::

:::example{17.1.10} Euclidean domains
- $\ZZ$, with $N(a) = |a|$ (division with remainder).
- $k[x]$ for a field $k$, with $N(f) = \deg f$. This is long division: if $a$ has leading term $\alpha x^m$ and $b$ has leading term $\beta x^n$ with $m \geq n$, then $a - \alpha\beta^{-1} x^{m-n} b$ has smaller degree than $a$, and repeating this gives $a = bq + r$ with $r = 0$ or $\deg r < \deg b$.
- The Gaussian integers ${\ZZ}[i]$, with $N(a + bi) = a^2 + b^2$ (Exercise [17.1](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings)(2)).
- The Eisenstein integers ${\ZZ}[\omega] = \{a + b\omega : a, b \in \ZZ\}$, where $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$, with $N(a + b\omega) = |a + b\omega|^2 = a^2 - ab + b^2$. The argument is the same as for ${\ZZ}[i]$, since every complex number lies within distance $1/\sqrt{3} < 1$ of an element of ${\ZZ}[\omega]$.
:::

## <span class="num">17.1.4</span> Principal Ideal Domains

:::definition{17.1.11} Principal ideal domain
An integral domain $R$ is a ***principal ideal domain*** (PID) if every ideal of $R$ is principal, that is, of the form $(a)$ for some $a \in R$.
:::

:::theorem{17.1.12} Every Euclidean domain is a PID
If $R$ is a Euclidean domain, then $R$ is a principal ideal domain.
:::

:::proof
Let $N$ be a Euclidean function and $I \subseteq R$ an ideal. If $I = 0$, then $I = (0)$. Otherwise choose $b \in I \setminus \{0\}$ with $N(b)$ minimal. Clearly $(b) \subseteq I$. For $a \in I$, write $a = bq + r$ with $r = 0$ or $N(r) < N(b)$. Since $r = a - bq \in I$, minimality forces $r = 0$, so $a = bq \in (b)$.
:::

In particular $\ZZ$, $k[x]$, ${\ZZ}[i]$ and ${\ZZ}[\omega]$ are principal ideal domains.

:::note
The converse fails: the ring ${\ZZ}\bigl[\tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-19}}{2}\bigr]$ is a principal ideal domain that has no Euclidean function (Motzkin, 1949).
:::

:::theorem{17.1.13} In a PID, irreducible $\iff$ prime
Let $R$ be a principal ideal domain and $p \in R$ a nonzero non-unit. Then $p$ is irreducible if and only if $p$ is prime.
:::

:::proof
($\Leftarrow$) This is Proposition [17.1.8](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#proposition-17-1-8).

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $p$ is irreducible and $p \mid ab$. Since $R$ is a PID, $(p, a) = (d)$ for some $d$. Then $d \mid p$, so $p = de$, and since $p$ is irreducible, either $d$ is a unit or $e$ is a unit. If $e$ is a unit, then $(d) = (p)$, so $a \in (p)$ and $p \mid a$. If $d$ is a unit, then $(p, a) = R$, so $1 = rp + sa$ for some $r, s \in R$, and $b = rpb + sab$; both terms are divisible by $p$, so $p \mid b$.
:::

:::corollary{17.1.14} Irreducible elements generate maximal ideals
If $R$ is a principal ideal domain and $p \in R$ is irreducible, then $(p)$ is a maximal ideal, so $R/(p)$ is a field.
:::

:::proof
Since $p$ is not a unit, $(p) \neq R$. If $(p) \subseteq J \subseteq R$ for an ideal $J = (d)$, then $d \mid p$, so $d$ is a unit (and $J = R$) or an associate of $p$ (and $J = (p)$). The last statement is Proposition [17.1.5](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#proposition-17-1-5).
:::

## <span class="num">17.1.5</span> Unique Factorization Domains

:::definition{17.1.15} Unique factorization domain
An integral domain $R$ is a ***unique factorization domain*** (UFD) if:

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. every nonzero non-unit $a \in R$ is a product of irreducible elements, $a = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n$; and
2. this factorization is unique up to order and associates: if $a = p_1 \cdots p_n = q_1 \cdots q_m$ with all $p_i, q_j$ irreducible, then $n = m$ and, after reordering, each $p_i$ is an associate of $q_i$.
:::

:::lemma{17.1.16} Ascending chains in a PID
In a principal ideal domain, every ascending chain of ideals $I_1 \subseteq I_2 \subseteq \cdots$ is eventually constant.
:::

:::proof
The union $I = \bigcup_n I_n$ is an ideal: if $a \in I_m$ and $b \in I_n$, then $a, b \in I_{\max(m,n)}$, so $a + b \in I$, and $ra \in I$ for all $r \in R$. So $I = (d)$ for some $d$, which lies in some $I_N$. Then $I = (d) \subseteq I_N \subseteq I_n \subseteq I$ for all $n \geq N$.
:::

:::theorem{17.1.17} Every PID is a UFD
Every principal ideal domain is a unique factorization domain.
:::

:::proof
*Existence.* Suppose some nonzero non-unit $a_0$ is not a product of irreducibles. Then $a_0$ is not irreducible, so $a_0 = bc$ with $b, c$ nonzero non-units, and one of $b, c$ is not a product of irreducibles (otherwise $a_0$ would be); call it $a_1$. Then $(a_0) \subsetneq (a_1)$: the inclusion holds since $a_0 = a_1 u$, where $u$ is the other factor, a non-unit; and if $(a_0) = (a_1)$, then $a_0 = a_1 v$ with $v$ a unit, and canceling $a_1$ would give $u = v$. Repeating the argument with $a_1$ in place of $a_0$, and so on, gives a strictly ascending chain $(a_0) \subsetneq (a_1) \subsetneq (a_2) \subsetneq \cdots$, contradicting Lemma [17.1.16](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#lemma-17-1-16).

*Uniqueness.* We use induction on $n$. Suppose $p_1 \cdots p_n = q_1 \cdots q_m$ with all factors irreducible. By Theorem [17.1.13](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#theorem-17-1-13), $p_n$ is prime, and since it divides the product $q_1 \cdots q_m$, it divides some $q_j$ (by induction on the number of factors). Reorder so that $j = m$. Then $q_m = p_n u$, and since $q_m$ is irreducible and $p_n$ is not a unit, $u$ is a unit: $p_n$ and $q_m$ are associates. Canceling $p_n$ gives $p_1 \cdots p_{n-1} = u q_1 \cdots q_{m-1}$. If $n = 1$, the left side is $1$, and since irreducibles are not units this forces $m = 1$. Likewise, if $m = 1$ then $n = 1$. Otherwise $uq_1$ is irreducible and an associate of $q_1$, and the induction hypothesis, applied to $p_1 \cdots p_{n-1} = (uq_1) q_2 \cdots q_{m-1}$, finishes the proof.
:::

:::example{17.1.18} Failure of unique factorization
In $R = {\ZZ}[\sqrt{-5}]$ we have $$6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5}).$$ The norm $N(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = |a + b\sqrt{-5}|^2 = a^2 + 5b^2$ is multiplicative: $N(\alpha\beta) = N(\alpha)N(\beta)$. If $\alpha$ is a unit, then $N(\alpha)N(\alpha^{-1}) = N(1) = 1$, so $N(\alpha) = 1$; and $a^2 + 5b^2 = 1$ only for $\pm 1$. So the units are $\pm 1$, and associates have the same norm. No element has norm 2 or 3, since $a^2 + 5b^2 \in \{2, 3\}$ has no integer solutions.

Now $N(2) = 4$, $N(3) = 9$, and $N(1 \pm \sqrt{-5}) = 6$. If one of these four elements were a product $\alpha\beta$ of two non-units, then $N(\alpha), N(\beta) > 1$ would be proper factors of 4, 9, or 6, so one of them would equal 2 or 3, which is impossible. So all four are irreducible. They are pairwise non-associate, having different norms, except $1 + \sqrt{-5}$ and $1 - \sqrt{-5}$, whose quotient is not $\pm 1$. So the two factorizations of 6 are genuinely different, and $R$ is not a UFD. In particular $2$ is irreducible but not prime: $2 \mid (1 + \sqrt{-5})(1 - \sqrt{-5})$, but $2$ divides neither factor, since $\frac{1 \pm \sqrt{-5}}{2} \notin R$.
:::

## <span class="num">17.1.6</span> Noetherian Rings

:::definition{17.1.19} Noetherian ring
A ring $R$ is ***Noetherian*** if it satisfies the ***ascending chain condition*** on ideals: every ascending chain $I_1 \subseteq I_2 \subseteq I_3 \subseteq \cdots$ of ideals of $R$ is eventually constant.
:::

:::proposition{17.1.20} Noetherian means finitely generated ideals
A ring $R$ is Noetherian if and only if every ideal of $R$ is finitely generated.
:::

:::proof
Suppose every ideal is finitely generated, and let $I_1 \subseteq I_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be a chain of ideals. As in the proof of Lemma [17.1.16](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#lemma-17-1-16), the union $I$ is an ideal. It is generated by finitely many elements, which all lie in some $I_N$; then $I \subseteq I_N$, and $I_n = I_N$ for $n \geq N$.

Conversely, suppose some ideal $I$ is not finitely generated. Choose $a_1 \in I$; since $(a_1) \neq I$, choose $a_2 \in I \setminus (a_1)$; since $(a_1, a_2) \neq I$, choose $a_3 \in I \setminus (a_1, a_2)$; and so on. Then $(a_1) \subsetneq (a_1, a_2) \subsetneq (a_1, a_2, a_3) \subsetneq \cdots$ is a chain that is never constant, so $R$ is not Noetherian.
:::

:::note
Every PID is Noetherian, since every ideal is generated by one element (or by Lemma [17.1.16](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#lemma-17-1-16)). In particular fields, $\ZZ$, and $k[x]$ are Noetherian. The polynomial ring $k[x_1, x_2, \ldots]$ in infinitely many variables is not: $(x_1) \subsetneq (x_1, x_2) \subsetneq (x_1, x_2, x_3) \subsetneq \cdots$.
:::

:::theorem{17.1.21} Hilbert Basis Theorem
If $R$ is a Noetherian ring, then so is the polynomial ring $R[x]$.
:::

:::proof
Let $I \subseteq R[x]$ be an ideal; by Proposition [17.1.20](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#proposition-17-1-20) we must show that $I$ is finitely generated. For $n \geq 0$, let $L_n \subseteq R$ be the set of coefficients of $x^n$ in the polynomials $f \in I$ with $f = 0$ or $\deg f \leq n$. Since $I$ is an ideal, $L_n$ is an ideal of $R$; its nonzero elements are the leading coefficients of the elements of $I$ of degree exactly $n$. If $f \in I$ has degree at most $n$, then $xf \in I$ has degree at most $n + 1$, and its coefficient of $x^{n+1}$ is the coefficient of $x^n$ in $f$; hence $L_0 \subseteq L_1 \subseteq L_2 \subseteq \cdots$. Since $R$ is Noetherian, there is an $N$ with $L_n = L_N$ for all $n \geq N$.

For each $n \leq N$, the ideal $L_n$ is finitely generated, so we may choose $f_{n,1}, \ldots, f_{n,k_n} \in I$, each zero or of degree at most $n$, whose coefficients of $x^n$ generate $L_n$. Let $J \subseteq I$ be the ideal generated by all the $f_{n,j}$ with $n \leq N$. We claim $J = I$. If not, choose $g \in I \setminus J$ of minimal degree $d$ (note $g \neq 0$), with leading coefficient $c$.

- If $d \leq N$, then $c \in L_d$, so $c = \sum_j r_j c_{d,j}$, where $c_{d,j}$ is the coefficient of $x^d$ in $f_{d,j}$. The polynomial $g - \sum_j r_j f_{d,j}$ lies in $I$, has degree less than $d$, and is not in $J$ (as $g \notin J$).
- If $d > N$, then $c \in L_d = L_N$, so $c = \sum_j r_j c_{N,j}$, and $g - \sum_j r_j x^{d-N} f_{N,j}$ lies in $I \setminus J$ and has degree less than $d$.

Either way the minimality of $d$ is contradicted. So $I = J$ is finitely generated.
:::

:::corollary{17.1.22} Polynomial rings in several variables
For any Noetherian ring $R$ and $n \geq 1$, the ring $R[x_1, \ldots, x_n] = R[x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}][x_n]$ is Noetherian. In particular $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ is Noetherian for every field $k$, and so is ${\ZZ}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$.
:::

## <span class="num">17.1.7</span> Polynomials over a Unique Factorization Domain

Gauss’s lemma compares factorizations in ${\ZZ}[x]$ and in ${\QQ}[x]$. A nonzero polynomial $f \in {\ZZ}[x]$ is ***primitive*** if no prime number divides all of its coefficients. Every nonzero $g \in {\QQ}[x]$ can be written as $g = c\,g_0$ with $c \in \QQ$ and $g_0 \in {\ZZ}[x]$ primitive: multiply $g$ by a common denominator $d$ of its coefficients, and divide $dg$ by the greatest common divisor $e$ of its coefficients, so that $c = e/d$.

:::lemma{17.1.23} Gauss’s lemma
The product of two primitive polynomials in ${\ZZ}[x]$ is primitive.
:::

:::proof
Let $f, g \in {\ZZ}[x]$ be primitive, and suppose a prime $p$ divides every coefficient of $fg$. Reducing coefficients mod $p$ is a ring homomorphism ${\ZZ}[x] \to ({\ZZ}/p)[x]$, $h \mapsto \bar{h}$, and $\bar{f}\bar{g} = \ol{fg} = 0$. Since ${\ZZ}/p$ is a field, $({\ZZ}/p)[x]$ is an integral domain, so $\bar{f} = 0$ or $\bar{g} = 0$. That is, $p$ divides every coefficient of $f$ or every coefficient of $g$, a contradiction.
:::

:::proposition{17.1.24} Factorizations over $\QQ$ and over $\ZZ$
If $f \in {\ZZ}[x]$ is a product $f = gh$ of nonconstant polynomials $g, h \in {\QQ}[x]$, then $f = g_1 h_1$ with $g_1, h_1 \in {\ZZ}[x]$, $\deg g_1 = \deg g$, and $\deg h_1 = \deg h$.
:::

:::proof
Write $g = a\,g_0$ and $h = b\,h_0$ with $a, b \in \QQ$ and $g_0, h_0 \in {\ZZ}[x]$ primitive. Then $f = ab\,g_0 h_0$, and $g_0 h_0$ is primitive by Gauss’s lemma. Write $ab = r/s$ in lowest terms with $s > 0$, so that $sf = r\,g_0h_0$. If a prime $p$ divides $s$, then $p$ divides every coefficient of $r\,g_0 h_0$; as $p \nmid r$, it divides every coefficient of $g_0 h_0$, which is impossible. So $s = 1$, and $f = (r g_0) h_0$.
:::

:::proposition{17.1.25} Eisenstein’s criterion
Let $f = a_n x^n + \cdots + a_1 x + a_0 \in {\ZZ}[x]$ with $n \geq 1$, and let $p$ be a prime such that $p \nmid a_n$, $p \mid a_i$ for all $i < n$, and $p^2 \nmid a_0$. Then $f$ is irreducible in ${\QQ}[x]$.
:::

:::proof
The units of ${\QQ}[x]$ are the nonzero constants, so if $f$ were reducible in ${\QQ}[x]$ it would be a product of two nonconstant polynomials, and by Proposition [17.1.24](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#proposition-17-1-24) we could write $f = gh$ with $g, h \in {\ZZ}[x]$ of degrees $r, s \geq 1$. The product of the leading coefficients of $g$ and $h$ is $a_n$, so $p$ divides neither of them, and the reductions mod $p$ satisfy $\deg \bar{g} = r$, $\deg \bar{h} = s$. Now $\bar{g}\bar{h} = \bar{f} = \bar{a}_n x^n$ in $({\ZZ}/p)[x]$. This ring is a Euclidean domain, hence a UFD (Theorems [17.1.12](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#theorem-17-1-12) and [17.1.17](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#theorem-17-1-17)), and $x$ is irreducible in it; so by unique factorization $\bar{g} = \beta x^r$ and $\bar{h} = \gamma x^s$ for some $\beta, \gamma \in {\ZZ}/p$. Since $r, s \geq 1$, the constant terms of $\bar{g}$ and $\bar{h}$ vanish, that is, $p$ divides the constant terms $g(0)$ and $h(0)$. Then $p^2$ divides $g(0)h(0) = a_0$, a contradiction.
:::

For instance, $x^3 - 2$, $x^4 - 2$, and $x^5 - 4x + 2$ are irreducible in ${\QQ}[x]$ (take $p = 2$).

The same ideas give a general theorem. For an integral domain $R$, the ***fraction field*** $\Frac(R)$ is built from $R$ as $\QQ$ is built from $\ZZ$ (and as $k(x)$ is built from $k[x]$ in Chapter 4): its elements are the fractions $a/b$ with $a, b \in R$, $b \neq 0$, where $a/b = a'/b'$ if and only if $ab' = a'b$.

:::theorem{17.1.26} Polynomial rings over a UFD
If $R$ is a unique factorization domain, then so is $R[x]$. In particular, ${\ZZ}[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ and $k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ (for a field $k$) are unique factorization domains.
:::

:::proof Proof (sketch)
In a UFD, greatest common divisors exist (up to units), so one can define primitive polynomials in $R[x]$ as above. Every prime element $p$ of $R$ gives an integral domain $R/(p)$ (Proposition [17.1.5](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#proposition-17-1-5)), so the proof of Gauss’s lemma works with $R$ in place of $\ZZ$, and so does Proposition [17.1.24](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#proposition-17-1-24), with $K = \Frac(R)$ in place of $\QQ$. It follows that the irreducible elements of $R[x]$ are the irreducible elements of $R$ and the primitive polynomials that are irreducible in $K[x]$. Factorizations in $R[x]$ are then obtained, and shown to be unique, from those in $R$ and in $K[x]$, which is a UFD because it is a Euclidean domain. The second statement follows by induction on $n$, since $R[x_1, \ldots, x_n] = R[x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}][x_n]$.
:::

:::note
We have shown the implications $$\text{Euclidean domain} \implies \text{PID} \implies \text{UFD} \implies \text{integral domain},$$ and none of them reverses. The ring ${\ZZ}\bigl[\tfrac{1 + \sqrt{-19}}{2}\bigr]$ is a PID but not Euclidean. The ring ${\ZZ}[x]$ is a UFD by Theorem [17.1.26](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#theorem-17-1-26) but not a PID: if $(2, x) = (f)$, then $f \mid 2$ forces $f = \pm 1$ or $\pm 2$, and $f \mid x$ forces $f = \pm 1$; but $1 \notin (2, x)$, since every element $2g + xh$ of $(2, x)$ has an even constant term. Finally ${\ZZ}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is an integral domain but not a UFD (Example [17.1.18](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#example-17-1-18)).
:::

:::exercise{17.1.27} Exercises
<!-- list:paren-decimal -->

1. Show that ${\ZZ}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a PID by finding an ideal that is not principal. (Hint: consider $(2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$.)
2. Prove that ${\ZZ}[i]$ is a Euclidean domain with $N(a + bi) = a^2 + b^2$. (The key step: for any $\alpha, \beta \in {\ZZ}[i]$ with $\beta \neq 0$, the quotient $\alpha/\beta \in \CC$ lies within distance $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} < 1$ of some Gaussian integer.)

:::solution
**(1)** Let $R = {\ZZ}[\sqrt{-5}]$ and $I = (2, 1 + \sqrt{-5})$. First, $I = \{a + b\sqrt{-5} : a \equiv b \pmod 2\}$. Indeed, the right side is an additive subgroup containing $2$ and $1 + \sqrt{-5}$, and it is closed under multiplication by $\sqrt{-5}$, since $\sqrt{-5}(a + b\sqrt{-5}) = -5b + a\sqrt{-5}$ and $-5b \equiv b \equiv a \pmod 2$; so it is an ideal containing $I$. Conversely, if $a \equiv b \pmod 2$, then $a + b\sqrt{-5} = b(1 + \sqrt{-5}) + (a - b)$ with $a - b \in (2)$, so it lies in $I$. In particular $1 \notin I$, and $I \neq R$.

Suppose $I = (\alpha)$. Then $\alpha \mid 2$ and $\alpha \mid 1 + \sqrt{-5}$, so by multiplicativity of the norm (Example [17.1.18](/notes/math-55a/17-1-commutative-rings#example-17-1-18)), $N(\alpha)$ divides $N(2) = 4$ and $N(1 + \sqrt{-5}) = 6$, hence divides 2. No element has norm 2, so $N(\alpha) = 1$, $\alpha = \pm 1$, and $I = R$, a contradiction. So $I$ is not principal.

**(2)** ${\ZZ}[i]$ is an integral domain, being a subring of $\CC$. Given $\alpha, \beta \in {\ZZ}[i]$ with $\beta \neq 0$, write $\alpha/\beta = u + vi$ with $u, v \in \QQ$. Choose integers $m, n$ with $|u - m| \leq \frac{1}{2}$ and $|v - n| \leq \frac{1}{2}$, and set $\gamma = m + ni$ and $r = \alpha - \beta\gamma \in {\ZZ}[i]$. Since $N(z) = |z|^2$ is multiplicative on $\CC$, $$N(r) = N(\beta)\,\Bigl|\frac{\alpha}{\beta} - \gamma\Bigr|^2 = N(\beta)\bigl((u - m)^2 + (v - n)^2\bigr) \leq \tfrac{1}{2} N(\beta) < N(\beta).$$ So $\alpha = \beta\gamma + r$ with $r = 0$ or $N(r) < N(\beta)$.
:::
:::
